title: Neonatal Resuscitation Principles and Neonatal Airway Management
path: Physiology and Care of the Newborn
Neonatal Resuscitation Principles and Neonatal Airway Management

headings.title: Introduction to Neonatal Resuscitation Principles
headings.content: Most newborns transition smoothly from intrauterine fluid-filled lungs to breathing air independently. However, roughly ten percent of babies require some level of assistance at birth, and about one percent need extensive resuscitation to survive without long-term harm. Midwives in Nigerian delivery suites must anticipate these needs by checking equipment before every single birth. The core principle of neonatal resuscitation focuses on establishing effective lung ventilation, because unlike adults whose cardiac arrest is primarily primary cardiac events, newborns suffer from asphyxia-related arrest. Opening and supporting the airway remains the absolute priority during every emergency intervention.

headings.title: The Golden Minute and Initial Assessment at Birth
headings.content: The first sixty seconds after birth are known as the **Golden Minute**. During this crucial window, the midwife must quickly evaluate three distinct parameters: term gestation, crying or breathing effort, and good muscle tone. If the baby is breathing well and has a strong cry, routine care involves skin-to-skin contact, drying, and keeping the infant warm. If the baby is gasping, limp, or born premature, immediate steps start right on the resuscitation table. Initial stabilization includes providing warmth, clearing the airway only if obstructed, drying the skin, stimulating breathing, and positioning the head correctly.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Newborn Airway
headings.content: A newborn airway possesses unique anatomical features that complicate management compared to an adult. The tongue is relatively large in proportion to the oral cavity, which can easily displace backward and block the pharynx. Furthermore, the infant's **larynx** sits higher and more anteriorly in the neck, and the **epiglottis** is long, narrow, and angled steeply over the glottic opening. The narrowest part of the pediatric airway is historically taught to be the **cricoid ring**, forming a natural seal beneath the vocal cords. Recognizing these structural differences prevents trauma during airway manipulation.

headings.title: Neonatal Airway Management Techniques and Positioning
headings.content: Proper head positioning opens the newborn airway by aligning the pharynx, larynx, and trachea. The midwife places the infant supine on a firm flat surface with the neck in a neutral or slightly extended position, often described as the **sniffing position**. Over-extension of the neck stretches the trachea and can actually close off the airway, while flexion pushes the chin into the chest and blocks airflow. Using a small rolled towel under the shoulders helps maintain this ideal alignment during ventilation.

headings.title: Clearing Secretions and Suctioning Protocols
headings.content: Routine suctioning of all newborns is no longer recommended, as gentle drying and stimulation usually clear normal fluid. Suctioning is reserved for babies who fail to breathe, have obvious airway obstructions from secretions, or require positive pressure ventilation. When suctioning is necessary, midwives use a bulb syringe or a mechanical suction catheter set at a safe negative pressure limit. The mouth is always cleared first before the nose to prevent the baby from gasping and inhaling pooled pharyngeal secretions. Vigorous deep suctioning inside the back of the throat must be avoided because it stimulates the vagus nerve and causes severe bradycardia.

headings.title: Positive Pressure Ventilation (PPV) and Monitoring Heart Rate
headings.content: If a newborn remains apneic, gasping, or has a heart rate below 100 beats per minute after initial steps, positive pressure ventilation must start within the Golden Minute. The midwife applies a properly sized face mask to cover the nose and mouth without pressing on the eyes or extending past the chin. An effective seal and correct head position are verified by watching for chest rise and listening for bilateral breath sounds. Heart rate assessment is the single most important indicator of successful resuscitation and is best measured using a stethoscope or pulse oximeter.

headings.title: Advanced Airway Interventions: Endotracheal Intubation and Laryngeal Masks
headings.content: When bag-mask ventilation fails to improve the newborn or prolonged resuscitation is required, advanced airway placement becomes necessary. Endotracheal intubation provides a secure airway, allows efficient chest compressions, and permits direct tracheal administration of medications if needed. The procedure requires a laryngoscope with a straight blade, appropriate sized endotracheal tubes, and a carbon dioxide detector to confirm proper tube placement in the trachea. Alternatively, **laryngeal mask airways** serve as an effective rescue device when intubation is difficult, fitting snugly over the laryngeal inlet.

headings.title: Post-Resuscitation Care and Continuous Evaluation
headings.content: Babies who require resuscitation face significant risks even after stable vital signs return. They must be transferred to a special care nursery or neonatal intensive care unit for continuous monitoring of temperature, blood glucose, breathing effort, and neurological status. Midwives must document all resuscitation events accurately, noting exact times of interventions, heart rate responses, and Apgar scores at one and five minutes. Ongoing observation prevents missed complications such as hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy or delayed respiratory distress.
